newsitem.title: USA: Barbie's newest friend arrives -in a pink wheelchair.
newsitem.headline: Barbie's newest friend arrives -in a pink wheelchair.

text.p: The makers of the Barbie doll on Wednesday introduced their newest creation -- a Barbie look-alike named Becky in a pink wheelchair.

"Showing children, regardless of what their different abilities are, they're really children all the same -- that's what we're trying to accomplish here," said Michael Goldstein, chief executive officer of Toys "R" Us, exclusive outlet for the new $19.95 doll.
"By having this doll in a wheelchair we will do a lot for children with different abilities," he said, adding that his company some time ago began calling disabled children "differently abled."

"We are very, very committed to portraying ... diversity," added Nancy Zwiers, senior vice president for Barbie marketing at Mattel Inc., which last year sold $1.7 billion worth of Barbie and related products worldwide.

The doll -- slim, busty and long-tressed like the rest of the Barbie family -- wears a blue-green denim skirt and jacket with matching shoes and headband and pink tights. Her pink wheelchair has wheels trimmed with iridescent mylar and comes with its own little backpack.

The auburn-haired doll named "Share a Smile Becky" was introduced at a news conference crowded with children and adults in wheelchairs, including former presidential press secretary Jim Brady, who was wounded in the assassination attempt on President Ronald Reagan in 1981.

"It's free enterprise at its best," said wheelchair-bound Justin Dart, a long-time activist for people with disabilities. "We're having a tough time trying to convince Congress to display FDR in a wheelchair and here we have free enterprise displaying Barbie in a wheelchair," he added.
Dart's reference was to the newly dedicated memorial in Washington to former president Franklin Delano Roosevelt which does not include a depiction of the polio-crippled president in a wheelchair.

Dart said later in an interview that even though there are plans being developed to add a wheelchair to the memorial, he and others still fear it will be "a little bas-relief thing" or in some other form that will attraction little attention.

The Barbie doll was developed with input from The National Parent Network on Disabilities and the National Lekotek Centre, the latter a group which provides special play centres for disabled children.
Except for the wheelchair and her clothes, the dolls is the same as any other in the line.

Mattel said Barbie is the world's best-selling doll and that the typical little girl in the United States owns 10 of them. Since her introduction 38 years ago, the original Barbie has been joined by a product line that includes a legion of friends and pets.
Goldstein said initial sales have been "phenomenal."
